title: The flip side and the dubbed tape of "Walking the Blues"
summary: McRae did a talking blues with Teacho Wiltshire for the other side and added rhythm by dubbing.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: So Glover says, "Hey, this is great, man. What are you gonna do on the other side?"
I say, "Well, I'll think of something."
I say, I'll go back in the studio and I'll do another side to it." He say, "Okay."
"You gonna use Jack?" I say, "No, I want to do an up tempo thing," you know.
Then I called Teacho Wiltshire and I said -- we got this thing with the piano, you know.
I say, "Do me a blues thing. Put it up tempo." And I told him (inaudible) started singing something to him (inaudible), you know.
And that's what I did on the other side. I did a talking think on the other side -- (inaudible) like a blues rhythm thing, you know.
"Yeah, man," you know. Just keep on

talking. He's playing and I'm just answering every once in a while -- come in with a line every once in a while, you know.
And we did that and we sent it out to Glover. Glover (and them inaudible) put some rhythm to it. The thing was a smash hit.
You mean you taped --
We did dub on it. Did a tape on it.
And then a dub was done on it.
Yeah. We did dub --
Was that one of the early instances of that sort of thing happening? Or was that fairly common in recording at that time?
Oh, we did a lot of that.
Oh, yeah?
We used to go in and make a -- like we was gonna make a record date -- we do a dub on it. We make a tape (of inaudible) just the rhythm. And they go and put the rhythm to it.
We say, 'Hey, that's good. Let's put
